THE ELECTRICAL AGE. APRIL, 1951

"The Electrical Age"

IN celebrating the centenary of the Great Exhibition of 1851 we are really commemorating the establishment of The Electrical Age itself, for most of the great developments of the last hundred years are dependent upon Faraday's discovery of electro-magnetic induction, from which all electrical applications derive. The Electrical Age can be studied in its several parts, among them industry, commerce, transport and communications, agriculture, health and healing, and especially the home; while doing so we realise that these parts are in fact indivisible.

BEHIND THE FESTIVAL SCENE
By PHYLLIS THOMPSON
South Bank Control Centre (“Electrical Review”)
BRITAIN’S five months of Festival are over, but the im- pressions it has created will live for another 100 years. With each person the lasting remembrance will be different, but dominant among them all is the effect of colour and light.

title: Captain
brief_context: His ship Discovery is mentioned as being lit for the Festival.
brief_extract: Mar- garet’s and the Abbey stood immobile and sombre as a back- ground will have a peculiarly satisfying memory for many a day to come. Under the subtle effects of electricity the beautiful becomes more beautiful and the plain takes on a Cinderella charm.

brief_extract: She is an excellent knitter and needlewoman, and a great reader. Miss Card joined the staff of the E.A.W. in 1933, after training at a Secretarial College.

title: Miss
brief_context: Pioneer E.A.W. member and teacher who mentored Miss Card.
brief_extract: in 1933, after training at a Secretarial College. She was fortunate in several factors—first and foremost in the fact that she had, for the first two years of her work with the Association, the advantage of working directly under a brilliant teacher — Miss Margaret Partridge, whom some of the older Branches will remember as a pioneer in the work of the E.A.W., and who was for this short time a member of the staff; secondly in the fact that she came to the Association at the point when the Electrical Handbook for Women was first envisaged, and her first job was to type this and help in its preparation for the printers. She was the "dog" on whom the manuscripts were "tried" from the point of view of understanding by non-technical students, and in this way gained a knowledge of elementary electricity which has stood her in good stead ever since; and thirdly that she joined the E.A.W.

title: Dame
brief_context: Founder of the International Women's Service Groups in London.
brief_extract: She is especially interested in international contacts and travel abroad, and apart from a week in camp spends most of her holidays on the Continent, where she has many friends. Some of these she first met during the war, when she was Secretary of the International Women's Service Groups in Great Britain, the organisation started by Dame Caroline for business and professional women of all nationalities in London at that time. She too is fond of reading, and is also very interested in the theatre.
